channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority delays vessel, truck and train movements and pushes scheduling onto manual processes at Latin America’s busiest port
item.category: Top Story
item.description: The Santos Port Authority (APS), which runs Brazil’s largest port, lost its internal IT systems on 6 November and confirmed a cyberattack on 10 November. Identification, access-control and digital port-operations tools went down, delaying vessel, truck and train movements, and route scheduling, vessel arrival records and billing were handled by hand. By 16 November the main systems were in final tests and about 70% of affected file backups had been recovered; vessel movements and port access continued throughout. CNN Brasil reports the malware was already on the network and activated after a 6 November power cut. The attacker and entry route are undisclosed, and the Federal Police are investigating. For railways serving ports, an authority’s IT outage reaches train scheduling and gate access, so the interchange needs a tested manual fallback (editorial assessment). - The Rio Times (16 Nov 2026, citing the Santos Port Authority); FreshPlaza (11 Nov 2026, vessel, truck and train delays; access-control impact); CyberDelegate (17 Nov 2026, citing Folha de S.Paulo, CNN Brasil and Agência Brasil; ~70% of backups recovered); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Outage from 6 Nov 2026; security level raised 8 Nov 2026; attack confirmed 10 Nov 2026; core systems in final tests 16 Nov 2026; investigation ongoing

item.title: [High] France expects EU sanctions on 14 December over Iran’s refrigeration sabotage as Iran-linked hackers turn to physical attacks
item.category: Incident — State-attributed sabotage of refrigeration controllers (France, Oct 2026); EU sanctions decision expected 14 Dec; WSJ reports Iran-linked sabotage at US water stations and aboard two tankers; no rail or transit victim reported
item.description: France’s foreign minister said on 17 November he expects EU foreign ministers to agree sanctions on 14 December against the people behind October’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration controllers. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit for the attack on about 700 French sites, which French authorities say caused at least 15 fires, and has sought arrest warrants for three officers; Iran rejects the accusations. Health-ISAC warned on 16 November that settings were also changed at French blood-service sites. US and Israeli officials have told the Wall Street Journal that Iran-linked hackers also sabotaged equipment at small Midwest water stations and aboard two tankers. No rail target is reported, but the same weak point, an internet-reachable controller with a default password, exists in station and depot building systems (editorial assessment). - Arab News, from AFP (17 Nov 2026, Barrot: EU decision expected 14 Dec); APA (18 Nov 2026, Barrot on France 5: sanctions within a month); dpa, via Yahoo News (16 Nov 2026, Kallas: EU sanctions in preparation); Asharq Al-Awsat and The New Arab (16 Nov 2026, French sanctions push); Health-ISAC (16 Nov 2026, cold-chain bulletin); Wall Street Journal (13 Nov 2026), via Newsmax wire on Yahoo News and Voice of Emirates; RFI via AOL (11 Nov 2026, Paris prosecutor’s warrant request); The Record (9 Nov 2026, French attribution and at least 15 fires); Insurance Journal, from Reuters (13 Nov 2026, BSI warning); Bytes Europe (13 Nov 2026, CCB warning); Midnight Blue (Nov 2026, AK-SM 800A research); GBHackers (13 Nov 2026); NPR (9 Nov 2026, Iranian denial); Iran International (14 Nov 2026, IRGC response); Arab News, from AFP (12 Nov 2026, Belgian statement) - Barrot: EU sanctions within a month 17–18 Nov 2026; EU confirms sanctions in preparation, French sanctions push and Health-ISAC bulletin 16 Nov 2026; WSJ report 13 Nov 2026; BSI and CCB warnings 13 Nov 2026; warrant request 11 Nov 2026; French attribution 9 Nov 2026; IRGC rejects French findings 14 Nov 2026; October attack 11–12 Oct 2026; investigations ongoing

item.title: [High] CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
item.category: Incident — CISA/FBI/HHS/USDA/DOT joint warning (5 Nov 2026) and a second wave of refrigeration attacks across about 11 European countries (1–4 Nov); Belgium says its evidence points to Iran (12 Nov), no formal attribution
item.description: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French stores were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost, and three French blood-service sites had settings changed with no blood lost. Belgium’s interior minister said on 12 November that evidence points to Iran, short of formal attribution (see the Iran sabotage card above); a pro-Russian claim is unverified. Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. If a controller is reachable from the internet, treat it as at risk today. - TechCrunch (5 Nov 2026, CISA/FBI joint statement); SentinelOne Labs (3 Nov 2026, updated 4 Nov); Cybersecurity Dive (3 Nov 2026, updated with 4 Nov developments); Unit 42 (6 Nov 2026, exposure counts); Censys (6 Nov 2026, exposure analysis); BleepingComputer (5 Nov 2026); Nextgov (29 Oct 2026); Al Jazeera (4 Nov 2026); CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-ALE-012; The Cyber Express (6 Nov 2026, CISA/FBI/HHS/USDA/DOT advisory summary); Industrial Cyber (6 Nov 2026); Help Net Security (6 Nov 2026); SecurityWeek (6 Nov 2026, hardening guidance); The Hacker News (9 Nov 2026, exposure trend); eBuilder Security (11 Nov 2026, Swedish government and NCSC warning); Arab News/AFP (12 Nov 2026, Belgian statement); Sekoia TDR (10 Nov 2026, second-wave technique) - Attacks overnight 1–2 Nov 2026; Germany, Romania and UK confirmed 4 Nov 2026; CISA/FBI joint warning 5 Nov 2026; French attribution of the October attack 9 Nov 2026; Swedish government warning 10 Nov 2026; Belgian minister points to Iran 12 Nov 2026 — investigations ongoing

item.title: [Medium] Maersk confirms hackers stole data from a legacy logistics system it inherited through an acquisition, as a ransomware group demands $5 million
item.category: Incident — Data theft from a legacy system Maersk inherited with LF Logistics, confirmed 11 Nov 2026; WhiteArmor claim (7 Nov) and $5M extortion demand unverified; no operational disruption reported
item.description: Maersk confirmed on 11 November that a threat actor breached a system belonging to LF Logistics, the Asian contract-logistics company it bought from Li & Fung in 2022, and took data. The WhiteArmor ransomware group listed Maersk on its leak site on 7 November, claims about 100 GB, including driver records with plaintext passwords and super-administrator accounts, and demands $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. Maersk says the incident is isolated to a local system, its evidence so far indicates no sensitive data was disclosed, there is no sign of impact on other systems or on customer API and EDI connections, and it does not expect operational disruption. It has not said when or how the intrusion happened. For freight and intermodal operators, systems inherited through acquisitions or run by partners are a common blind spot (editorial assessment). - BleepingComputer (11 Nov 2026, Maersk confirmation and WhiteArmor demand); SecurityWeek (Nov 2026, Maersk statement of 11 Nov); rail and intermodal relevance is our editorial assessment - Leak-site listing 7 Nov 2026; Maersk confirmation 11 Nov 2026; investigation ongoing

item.title: [Critical] Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
item.category: Incident — PHP2Shell plus Gaia root flaw CVE-2026-123039 used to backdoor Check Point gateways and wipe a VMware ESXi host (wave 1 from 30 Oct, Israel; wave 2 from 2 Nov, multiple countries); CVE-2026-123039 added to CISA KEV 13 Nov 2026
item.description: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these gateways often guard remote access into rail control centres, and ESXi often hosts SCADA, passenger-information and crew systems (editorial assessment). - Check Point Research (12 Nov 2026); SecurityWeek (13 Nov 2026); Canadian Centre for Cyber Security AV26-1154 (12 Nov 2026, updated 13 Nov); CISA KEV alert (13 Nov 2026); BleepingComputer (Nov 2026) - Wave 1 from 30 Oct 2026; wave 2 from 2 Nov 2026; research published 12 Nov 2026; KEV addition 13 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
item.category: Government threat assessment — DHS Secretary’s written testimony to the House Homeland Security Committee (18 Nov 2026); DNI and DHS tell the same hearing recent US outages were not cyberattacks
item.description: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems and poor cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions, which officials tie to software defects and upgrade failures. Separately, AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For rail and transit, transportation is now named in the official US threat picture (editorial assessment). - Jerusalem Post (18 Nov 2026, Mullin written testimony); Report.az (18 Nov 2026); Bloomberg (18 Nov 2026); Federal News Network (18 Nov 2026, outages not a coordinated attack); Washington Examiner (18 Nov 2026, hearing); AttackIQ “Weighing Cyber Power”, via Water Online (17 Nov 2026) - Testimony and hearing 18 Nov 2026; AttackIQ research 17 Nov 2026

item.title: [Medium] Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
item.category: Research — Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis for Q3 2026 (published 16 Nov 2026), covering July–September; Check Point October 2026 statistics (12 Nov 2026) for comparison
item.description: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims jumped from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105); oil and gas logged 47. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total; transport and logistics, the third-largest group, is where rail and intermodal operators sit. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Check Point separately counted a record 1,063 claimed victims across all sectors in October. - Dragos (16 Nov 2026); Australian Cyber Security Magazine (17 Nov 2026); Check Point Research October 2026 statistics, via iTWire (12 Nov 2026) - Published 16 Nov 2026; data covers July–September 2026

item.title: [High] Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train”: Lumen exposes the throwaway relay chains the China-linked group uses to exploit SD-WAN and IT-management platforms — and lists rail among the sectors targeted
item.category: Threat intelligence — Lumen Black Lotus Labs research on Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” relay framework (28 Oct 2026); rail named among targeted sectors; no victims named
item.description: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs said on 28 October that the China-linked group Volt Typhoon has used a framework it calls “Silent Train” since November 2023 to reach targets without exposing its own infrastructure. Each operation runs through a fresh chain of typically four to six hops — rented servers abroad, then compromised small-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise appliances — assembled in under two minutes and cleaned up afterwards. The chains are aimed at management and control-plane platforms: Lumen ties the group to exploitation of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN CVE-2026-20127, VeloCloud Orchestrator CVE-2026-16812, N-able N-central CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, Versa Director and, with moderate confidence, a Quest KACE zero-day. Lumen names rail among the critical-infrastructure sectors targeted. No victim is named and no OT access is described; the N-central flaws matter again as new N-central chains are exploited (see Critical Advisories). - Lumen Black Lotus Labs research; corroborated by CyberScoop and Zero Day (Kim Zetter); KEV status of the named CVEs per the CISA catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release) as mirrored by CIRCL; CVSS per Cisco as CNA; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Lumen report and coverage 28 Oct 2026 (Zero Day clarified on 30 Oct that the relay servers were rented, not compromised); activity observed from Nov 2023

item.title: [Medium] ESET documents a Belarus-aligned group’s first destructive attack in Europe — on a Ukrainian manufacturer with an important role in the country’s transportation sector
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Vendor APT reporting; destructive attacks in Ukraine, one victim with a transportation role
item.description: ESET’s APT Activity Report covering April to September 2026, published on 28 October, says that according to its telemetry the Belarus-aligned group it tracks as FrostyNeighbor attacked a manufacturing company in Ukraine that plays an important role in the country’s transportation sector, and calls it the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned actor that ESET has documented in the European theatre. ESET does not name the company, the malware or the date, and describes no effect on transport operations. The same report notes the Iran-aligned OilRig subgroup FilthyFeline taking over activity against a cellular data provider in Uzbekistan, and North Korea’s DeceptiveDevelopment moving from fake job interviews to compromising source-code repositories with stolen developer credentials. Six days earlier, on 22 October, ESET described how the Russia-aligned UAC-0099 gained access to a Ukrainian grain firm through a spearphishing attachment in July 2025, after which Sandworm wiped data there in September 2025 by pushing a deletion tool through Active Directory Group Policy; ESET assesses that UAC-0099 can act as an initial-access group for Sandworm. All attributions are ESET’s assessments. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: transport manufacturers and freight logistics are now inside the destructive-attack target set in this conflict, and a wipe pushed through Group Policy reaches every domain-joined machine, including those that support operations. - ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q3 2026; ESET research on MythicRatatoskr (UAC-0099 and Sandworm); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - MythicRatatoskr research 22 Oct 2026 (intrusion Jul–Sep 2025); APT Activity Report 28 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
item.category: Active exploitation — VMware vCenter authentication bypass CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) exploited as a zero-day for more than two months by a suspected China-linked group, per Mandiant; Broadcom fix released 19 Nov 2026; no public fix for vCenter 7.0
item.description: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, moved to Linux appliances, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, created an SSO admin account, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Rail control centres often run SCADA servers, passenger-information and crew systems as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment). - SecurityWeek (19 Nov 2026, citing Broadcom, Google Threat Intelligence/Mandiant and Mandiant CTO Charles Carmakal); CISA KEV alert (20 Nov 2026); The Hacker News (20–21 Nov 2026) - Added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; patched 19 Nov 2026; exploited from at least early Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
item.category: Active exploitation — Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 9.8), clustered Expressway Core/Edge; exploited after a public PoC (reported by F6); added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; fixed in X15.5.20
item.description: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network, and gained root. From there they ran Python scripts, which F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing, to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 20 November alongside the vCenter zero-day. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported, but Expressway is a perimeter gateway that often bridges outside callers into internal networks, so an exposed, unpatched cluster is a foothold close to control-centre systems (editorial assessment). - Security Affairs (21 Nov 2026, CISA KEV additions of 20 Nov); SecurityWeek (Nov 2026, citing F6); Security Affairs (20 Nov 2026, F6 findings) - Added to CISA KEV 20 Nov 2026; exploitation reported 18–20 Nov 2026; patched 21 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
item.category: Active exploitation — PHP2Shell chained with a Linux kernel flaw to root exposed PAN-OS firewalls, 23–24 Oct; OT vendor advisories 28–30 Oct; Siemens adds metering gateways 16 Nov
item.description: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT operator is named. Where railways run these grid-control and RTU products for traction power, or RUGGEDCOM APE1808 in wayside networks, treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning (editorial assessment). - Unit 42 (updated 29 Oct 2026); Palo Alto Networks advisory for CVE-2026-109618 (updated 29 Oct 2026); The Record (29 Oct 2026) and Infosecurity Magazine (30 Oct 2026), citing Dream; CISA KEV catalog (30 Oct 2026 release); Siemens SSA-166980 V1.4 (16 Nov 2026, WTV676/WTV776 added; V1.2 29 Oct 2026), SSA-566512 V1.1 (28 Oct 2026), SSA-019113 and SSA-082556; Schneider Electric SESB-2026-295-01 v3.2.0 (30 Oct 2026); ABB Netcontrol and Arctic advisories (30 Oct 2026), ASPECT advisory (29 Oct 2026) and APROL SA26P015 (23 Oct 2026); CERT@VDE VDE-2026-127 and VDE-2026-137 - Root compromises 23–24 Oct 2026, verified by Unit 42 29 Oct 2026; KEV additions 26 and 28 Oct 2026; Siemens, Schneider and ABB updates 28–30 Oct 2026; Siemens metering gateways added 16 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] Siemens says the KEV-listed Node2Shell flaw reaches WinCC, WinCC OA and TIA Administrator, most with no fix yet, and flags an unfixable NTLM weakness in WinCC and PCS 7
item.category: Advisory — Siemens SSA-242944 (Node2Shell, CVE-2026-111497, CVSS 9.8) and SSA-970803 (NTLM relay, CVE-2026-58114, CVSS 7.5), released 10 Nov 2026; republished by CISA as ICSA-26-321-03 and ICSA-26-321-08 on 17 Nov 2026; many WinCC versions without a fix
item.description: Siemens has confirmed that Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497, CVSS 9.8), the Brotli decoder flaw CISA added to KEV on 27 October, affects a long list of its industrial software; CISA republished the advisory as ICSA-26-321-03 on 17 November. Fixes exist for SIMATIC WinCC OA V3.20 (P17.1), Braumat and Sistar. WinCC V7/V8, WinCC Runtime Professional, WinCC Unified PC Runtime, WinCC OA V3.21, TIA Administrator and User Management Component have no fix yet, and Siemens advises disabling Brotli compression where it is not needed. A second advisory (ICSA-26-321-08) covers CVE-2026-58114: WinCC, PCS 7 V9.1 and Process Historian still accept deprecated NTLM authentication, so an on-path attacker can relay a user’s login; several products will get no fix. Neither flaw is reported exploited against Siemens products. WinCC and WinCC OA run in some station, tunnel and traction-power SCADA (editorial assessment). - Siemens SSA-242944 and SSA-970803 as republished by CISA in ICSA-26-321-03 and ICSA-26-321-08 (17 Nov 2026, mirrored by DEFCONLevel); SecurityWeek ICS Patch Tuesday (Nov 2026); BleepingComputer (28 Oct 2026, KEV listing); CISA ICS bulletin (12 Nov 2026) for the RUGGEDCOM APE1808 advisories ICSA-26-316-04/-05; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Siemens advisories 10 Nov 2026; CISA republication 17 Nov 2026; Node2Shell in KEV 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
item.category: Advisory — OpenJDK “Java4Shell” memory-corruption flaw CVE-2026-114938 (disclosed and patched 17 Nov 2026); exploitation attempts seen 18–19 Nov 2026; Siemens SSA-272816 lists three Industrial Edge Management products
item.description: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched. - SecurityWeek (19 Nov 2026, citing Calif, GreyNoise, WatchTowr, Cloudflare, Previdian, Siemens SSA-272816, Cisco and Atlassian); The Record (18 Nov 2026, CISA alert) - Disclosed and patched 17 Nov 2026; exploitation attempts 18–19 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
item.category: Active exploitation — N-able N-central: 4EverAble2Shell exploited to plant miners (13 Nov 2026); N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 fixes 17 more CVEs and removes the Legacy API (16–17 Nov 2026); separate breach of N-able’s hosted Mail Assure/SpamExperts cloud disclosed 20 Nov 2026
item.description: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November, which it calls a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, missing authorization checks, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and it removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which N-able warns can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2. Remote control and Intune integration stay blocked for now. Separately, N-able said on 20 November that attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts email-filtering cloud, forcing it to take the management portal and APIs offline; it says mail flow continued, it has found no access to customer data, and the breach is unrelated to N-central. Many integrators manage control-centre and depot Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment). - BleepingComputer (20 Nov 2026, Mail Assure/SpamExperts breach); The Hacker News (17 Nov 2026, Hotfix 3, citing N-able release notes of 16 Nov); The Hacker News (13 Nov 2026, citing Huntback and Previdian); The Hacker News (12 Nov 2026, new chains); SecurityWeek (13 Nov 2026); Tenable (10 Nov 2026) - Mail Assure breach disclosed 20 Nov 2026; Hotfix 3 released 16 Nov 2026; exploitation reported 13 Nov 2026; Able2Shell disclosed 9 Nov 2026

item.title: [High] Cisco ASA and FTD: an exploited zero-day lets an unauthenticated attacker reload the remote-access VPN firewall — in KEV, the 1 November federal deadline now passed, and no workaround
item.category: Critical Advisory — Boundary firewall and remote-access VPN, exploited denial-of-service zero-day, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 on 28 October for CVE-2026-76418 in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) software, and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in October. Where SSL VPN is enabled and a tunnel group — DefaultWEBVPNGroup included — is configured with secondary authentication, a crafted request from a remote, unauthenticated attacker makes the device reload; Cisco notes that a successful VPN login is not needed to reach the vulnerable code. Cisco scores it CVSS v3.1 8.6. It is a denial of service, not code execution, but each reload drops every VPN session and whatever else the firewall carries until it restarts. There are no workarounds: Cisco’s mitigation is to disable the tunnel-group list or remove secondary authentication, which it says weakens the VPN’s security. Fixed releases are ASA 9.16.4.104, 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48 and 9.24.1.27 or 9.24.10.1, and FTD 7.0.11, 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3 and 10.1.1. CISA added it to KEV on 29 October with a 1 November federal deadline, which has passed. Cisco has not named the attackers or described targets, and no rail or transit victim has been reported. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: ASA and FTD are common at railway IT/OT boundaries and as the VPN that remote engineers and suppliers use, secondary authentication is exactly the stronger login operators add for that access, and older ASA and FTD flaws are among the entry routes in the SafePay advisory on this page. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75 (v1.0); CISA KEV entry via the CVE record on CIRCL (30 Oct 2026 catalogue); The Hacker News; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory 28 Oct 2026; added to KEV 29 Oct 2026; federal due date 1 Nov 2026

item.title: [Critical] Arista patches a third exploited VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day in four months, and CISA adds it to KEV — the console that configures the SD-WAN edge at every connected site
item.category: Critical Advisory — SD-WAN orchestrator, vendor-confirmed exploited zero-day; in KEV since 23 Oct
item.description: Arista disclosed on 22 October that CVE-2026-114625, an SQL injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator, was detected by Arista and is known to be actively exploited. Any authenticated user, down to the lowest built-in tenant role, can use it to gain operator privileges and act as a local “superuser operator”. Arista, as CVE numbering authority, rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4. Fixed releases are 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12; Arista-hosted and dedicated orchestrators are already patched, and VeloCloud gateways and edges are not affected. SecurityWeek lists two IP addresses seen in the attacks and quotes Arista: “There is no configuration that can prevent the exposure,” so updating is the remedy. It is the third exploited orchestrator zero-day in four months, after CVE-2026-16812 in July and CVE-2026-93952 in September, and CISA added it to KEV late on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, which has passed; an earlier edition of this page wrongly showed it as not listed. No victims, sectors or actor have been named for CVE-2026-114625; Lumen’s Silent Train report (see Threat Intelligence & Research) ties Volt Typhoon to the July flaw, CVE-2026-16812, not to this one. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: where stations, depots and wayside sites hang off an SD-WAN, the orchestrator holds the configuration of every edge, so whoever controls it can reroute traffic or open paths into the networks behind them. - Arista security advisory 0199 as reflected in the CVE record (Arista as CNA) and reported by SecurityWeek and The Hacker News; CISA KEV catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Disclosed and patched 22 Oct 2026; added to KEV 23 Oct 2026; earlier exploited VCO zero-days July and Sept 2026

item.title: [High] The Linux kernel flaw used to root PAN-OS firewalls, CVE-2026-46300, is in KEV — and Siemens lists it in the Linux subsystem of S7-1500 MFP controllers, fixed in V3.1.7 but not for V3.1.5
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited Linux kernel privilege escalation, KEV-listed; OT bridge through Siemens S7-1500 MFP; local access required
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-46300, a Linux kernel flaw that Infosecurity Magazine and Cybersecurity Dive call “Fragnesia”, to KEV on 28 October with a 31 October federal deadline, now passed. When the kernel coalesces network-buffer fragments it can drop a marker that says they are shared, so ESP decryption runs in place over page-cache data and a low-privileged local user can write to the cached contents of files they should only be able to read, potentially gaining root. Red Hat scores it CVSS v3.1 7.8, and it is fixed upstream in 5.10.257, 5.15.208, 6.1.174, 6.6.141, 6.12.91, 6.18.33 and 7.0.10. CISA’s KEV entry says it can be chained with the PHP2Shell flaws to plant PHP web shells and run commands as root, and The Record and Infosecurity identify it as the kernel step in the PAN-OS compromises described in the PHP2Shell card above. On its own it is a local flaw: it does not let anyone in from the network, but it turns any foothold into root. The OT bridge is Siemens. Its advisories SSA-019113 and SSA-082556 cover the additional GNU/Linux subsystem of the SIMATIC S7-1500 CPU 1518(F)-4 PN/DP MFP: Siemens lists CVE-2026-46300 for V3.1.6, fixed by updating to V3.1.7 or later, while V3.1.5 has no fix and is no longer maintained, leaving Siemens’ mitigations of running only trusted applications and restricting access to the Linux subsystem’s shell. No exploitation of a Siemens product has been reported. Keep it separate from CVE-2026-43284, a similar kernel flaw with public exploit code listed in Hitachi Energy’s CoreTec advisory, which is not in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: S7-1500 controllers run depot, workshop, tunnel-ventilation and station plant, and many trackside, telemetry and on-board gateways run embedded Linux, where a flaw like this turns a low-privileged foothold into full control of the device. - CISA KEV entry and CVE record via CIRCL (30 Oct 2026 catalogue); Siemens ProductCERT SSA-019113 and SSA-082556; chain reporting by The Record and Infosecurity Magazine; CVSS per Red Hat; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - CVE published 23 May 2026; added to KEV 28 Oct 2026; named in the PAN-OS chain 29 Oct 2026; federal due date 31 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa fixes a man-in-the-middle flaw in its Remote Connect client — but its OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway is end-of-life, with static keys and an SMS command-injection flaw that will not be fixed
item.category: Advisory — Remote-access client and cellular gateway flaws; one product end-of-life with no fix; no reported exploitation
item.description: Moxa published advisory MPSA-269510 on 27 October for three flaws. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, Moxa) affects the MRC Client of Moxa Remote Connect Suite, versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0: because the client does not properly validate certificates when it takes an OpenVPN configuration supplied by the server, an attacker positioned between client and server could impersonate the server and read or alter the connection. Version 4.2.2 is not affected and, according to CERT-FR, the fix is obtained through Moxa technical support. The other two affect the OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway: CVE-2026-111460 (v4.0 7.7), private keys for HTTPS and the device certificate authority embedded statically in the firmware, and CVE-2026-111461 (v4.0 7.5), an operating-system command injection that an attacker with the required privileges can reach when SMS management is enabled. The gateway is end-of-life and no fix will be issued; Moxa’s mitigations are to reset the device so it regenerates its keys and to keep SMS management disabled, which is the default. No exploitation has been reported, and none of the three is in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: Moxa networking and cellular equipment is common across railways — on rolling stock, at stations and in wayside and telemetry cabinets — and remote-access clients like MRC are how engineers reach those sites from outside. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-269510; CVE records with Moxa as CNA, via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-AVI-1393 for end-of-life status and fix distribution; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s 22–29 October ICS releases are light for rail: ICONICS SCADA products with three legacy lines that will never be fixed, two Hitachi Energy devices, EPICS Base and a video encoder
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS releases of 22, 27 and 29 Oct; no transport label; no reported exploitation
item.description: Beyond its republication of Siemens’ October advisories, covered in the Siemens card below, the CISA ICS advisories we could confirm for the window are six. ICSA-26-300-02 (27 October) republishes Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory 2026-006 of 15 October: CVE-2026-16438, an incorrect privilege assignment rated CVSS v3.1 9.1, two weak password-recovery flaws (CVE-2026-16436 at 8.1 and CVE-2026-16437 at 6.4) and the libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (8.2), across GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI, IoTWorX, MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz. GENESIS 11.04 and release 10.98 of the GENESIS64 family fix them, but no fix is planned for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz, which Mitsubishi Electric says should be replaced; meanwhile it advises replacing the password-recovery challenge file with a blank one and restricting write access to it. ICSA-26-300-01 (27 October) covers four network-reachable flaws in EPICS Base 7.0.10 and earlier, the open-source control toolkit used at accelerators and research facilities, including an integer overflow rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 / v4.0 9.3 (CVE-2026-114595); 7.0.11 fixes them. ICSA-26-295-01 (22 October) covers nine flaws in the Kiloview E3 video encoder, fixed in firmware 1.30. On 29 October CISA added three more. ICSA-26-302-02 covers Hitachi Energy TRO600 series firmware: CVE-2026-106087 lets an unauthenticated attacker read or download arbitrary files, including configuration and password data (CVSS v3.1 7.5 per CISA, v4.0 8.7 per Hitachi Energy), and CVE-2026-10756 lets an authenticated attacker use port forwarding to reach services bound to localhost (v3.1 7.5); 9.2.2.1 fixes both. ICSA-26-302-03 covers Hitachi Energy CoreTec 4 and 5: an authenticated command injection (CVE-2026-13162) and, on CoreTec5, the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-43284, for which public exploit code exists. CISA lists CoreTec5 5.0.0 as the fix and migration to CoreTec5 for CoreTec4, but the CVE record also lists 5.0.0 as affected, so check Hitachi Energy’s notice. ICSA-26-302-01 republishes Siemens’ Mendix SAML module advisory, a replay flaw rated CVSS v3.1 6.8. CISA lists Critical Manufacturing, not transportation, for the two 27 October advisories and Energy for the two Hitachi Energy advisories, and reports no known exploitation for any of the six. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: ICONICS software turns up as the HMI and energy-monitoring layer in facilities, including stations, depots and control buildings, and unfixable legacy lines are exactly what lingers in long-lived installations; Hitachi Energy equipment can sit in the substations that feed traction power, so the two Hitachi Energy advisories are worth a check even without a transport label. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-295-01, ICSA-26-300-01, ICSA-26-300-02 and ICSA-26-302-01 to -03, read via CISA’s CSAF data as mirrored by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; Mitsubishi Electric advisory 2026-006; KEV status per the CISA catalogue (30 Oct 2026 release) via CIRCL; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Mitsubishi Electric advisory 15 Oct 2026; Kiloview advisory 22 Oct 2026; ICONICS republication and EPICS Base advisory 27 Oct 2026; Hitachi Energy and Mendix republications 29 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] UK transport strategy asks operators to build cyber resilience into continuity plans, citing a £1.8bn cost for a week-long cyber outage of rail communications
item.category: Regulation & Policy — UK Department for Transport Transport Resilience Strategy (2 Nov 2026); cites KPMG’s £1.8bn systemic rail cyber-incident scenario; no new legal obligations
item.description: The UK Department for Transport published its Transport Resilience Strategy on 2 November, with 22 commitments for the next five to ten years, including transport resilience standards, a Transport Resilience Network and a Transport Resilience Academy pilot. On cyber, it asks operators to make cyber resilience part of business-continuity planning by identifying vulnerabilities, mapping interdependencies and setting up response and recovery arrangements, aligned with the government’s National Cyber Action Plan. It cites KPMG research estimating that a reasonable-worst-case cyber incident on Network Rail’s train communications system, causing a week of disruption, could cost about £1.8bn: roughly £123.5m to Network Rail, £281.3m in passenger delay and £1.4bn in wider economic impact. In the scenario ETCS Level 2 services stop until systems are restored and other trains are slowed. KPMG rated the chance of systemic disruption within two years as low. - GOV.UK, Transport Resilience Strategy (2 Nov 2026); Railway-News (11 Nov 2026, KPMG figures and scenario); Megaproject (12 Nov 2026); KPMG/DSIT figures also reported by ITPro (29 Jun 2026); rail relevance is direct - Strategy published 2 Nov 2026; KPMG research produced 2025

item.title: [Info] CISA’s four-year strategy, “CISA 2030”, puts operational technology and consequence-based prioritisation at its centre — with a review of core services due to start within 60 days
item.category: Regulation & Policy — CISA four-year strategy; OT named as a priority; no new obligations
item.description: CISA released its strategic plan, CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, on 26 October. Acting Director Nick Andersen describes a shift from passive defence to an anticipatory stance, and the plan says the agency will move away from threat-agnostic, all-hazards approaches toward risk-informed, consequence-based analysis. It names OT security — asset visibility and intrusion detection — among its priorities, alongside third-party and supply-chain guidance and support for a national risk register. CISA will begin a review of its core services within 60 days, deliver an implementation plan with metrics within 180 days and report progress after a year. The plan creates no new legal authorities and no new obligations for operators. Analysts quoted by GovInfoSecurity question how quickly the agency can deliver it with reduced staffing. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: a consequence-based CISA is likely to start conversations by asking which systems would hurt most if lost, and operators who have already ranked their own — dispatch, signalling support, traction power, passenger information — will be better placed in those conversations and in their TSA assessments. - CISA strategic plan as reported by Cybersecurity Dive, Nextgov/FCW, CyberScoop and GovInfoSecurity (cisa.gov could not be fetched); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Released 26 Oct 2026; core-services review to begin within 60 days
